source_text: Si quis dixerit, Christum sola opinione atque fictitie apparuisse mundo; et non confessus fuerit ipsum in carne venisse; anathema sit. Quomodo potest quispiam dicere, Christum putatitie ac ficte apparuisse mundo; Christum dico, in Bethleem natum, ad circumcisionem carnis adductum, a Symeone gestatum; usque ad duodecimum annum a parentibus educatum, iisque morigerum; in Iordane baptizatum, in cruce confixum, et a mortuis suscitatum? Quamobrem dum dicitur: Turbatus est spiritu, tristatus est anima, vulneratus est corpore; appellationes passionum secundum naturae nostrae constitutionem asserit, ut ostendat se hominem in mundo esse natum, et cum hominibus conversatum ad similitudinem nostram, sine tamen peccato. Natus est enim in Bethleem secundum carnem, ut Deum decebat, Angelis caelestibus Dominum suum agnoscentibus, et Deum in praesepio pannis involutum collaudantibus, atque dicentibus: Gloria in altissimis Deo, et in terra pax hominibus bonae voluntatis. In Nazaret enutritus est. In medio Doctorum sedens, Deum se ostendit, et admirationem eis movit super sapientia praeter tempus aetatis, secundum corpus, sicut Evangelicus sermo enarrat. In Iordane baptizatus est, non ut sanctificationem assumeret, sed ut sanctificationis participationem aliis elargiretur. In deserto tentatus est, non subiectus tentationi: sed nostras tentationes provocationi tentatoris obiiciens; ut vanum esse tentantem demonstraret. Propterea ait: Confidite, ego vici mundum. Non divinam luctationem opponens; sed propriam carnem victricem passionis, et mortis, atque corruptionis ostendens: ut per quam carnem, peccatum intravit in mundum, et per peccatum mors in omnibus hominibus regnavit; per eandem carnem secundum similitudinem, damnaretur peccatum in carne; et vinceretur peccati praeses qui tentat; et mors dissolveretur, ne regnaret; et corruptio in corporis sepultura evanesceret; primitiaeque resurrectionis ostenderentur, et principium iustitiae in mundo per fidem exerceretur; regnumque caelorum hominibus adnunciaretur, et Dei cum hominibus communio iniretur. Pro hac gratia glorificemus patrem, qui dedit filium suum unigenitum pro mundi vita: glorificemus spiritum sanctum, qui operatur in nobis et vivificat nos, et charismata ad communionem cum Deo ineundam tribuit: et ne doctrinam Evangelicam curiose verbis aridis perscrutemur, interminatas quaestiones et pugnas verborum circunferentes; et planum ac facilem, rectumque de fide sermonem, asperum reddentes: sed potius operemur opus fidei, pacem amemus, concordiam praeferamus, unitatem atque coniunctionem servemus, charitatem excolamus, per quam placatur Deus. Quemadmodum autem nostrum non est, scire tempora aut momenta quae pater posuit in sua potestate; credere autem oportet, finem fore huius temporis, et futuram venturi saeculi manifestationem, ac iudicii revelationem, et filii Dei adventum, operumque retributionem, ac hereditatis regni caelorum possessionem: sic non est nostrum scire, quomodo filius Dei factus sit homo. Mysterium enim hoc magnum est, sicut scriptum est, Generationem eius quis enarrabit? quia tollitur de terra vita eius. Sed credere oportet, quod filius Dei factus sit homo secundum Scripturas; et quod in terra visus sit, et cum hominibus conversatus, ut scripturae docent, ad similitudinem nostram, absque peccato; quodque pro nobis mortuus sit, et resurrexit ex mortuis, sicut scriptum est; et quod in caelos assumptus sit, sedetque in dextera patris, unde venturus est iudicare vivos et mortuos, sicut Scriptura docet: ne forte dum verbis inter nos contendimus, blasphement quidam doctrinam fidei; eveniatque quod dictum est: Propter vos semper blasphematur nomen meum in gentibus.
thought_title: Anathema against docetism; Christ's real life, passion, and victory through flesh; doxology; call to simple faith and conduct; mystery of the incarnation; warning against word-strife
orientation: Gregory closes the treatise by anathematizing anyone who says Christ only seemed to appear, then recounts the concrete events of Christ's life to prove his real humanity, explains how his flesh wins victory over sin and death, offers a trinitarian doxology, urges believers to pursue faith's works rather than curious word-battles, affirms the mystery of the incarnation, and warns that disputing over words blasphemes the faith.
pass_a_gloss: If anyone shall have said that Christ appeared to the world only in opinion and fictitiously; and shall not have confessed that he himself came in flesh; let him be anathema. How can anyone say that Christ appeared to the world supposedly and fictitiously; I say Christ, born in Bethlehem, led to circumcision of flesh, carried by Simeon; reared up to the twelfth year by parents, and obedient to them; baptized in the Jordan, fixed on a cross, and raised from the dead? Wherefore while it is said: He was troubled in spirit, he was saddened in soul, he was wounded in body; it asserts the names of passions according to the constitution of our nature, that he may show himself to be a man born in the world, and to have conversed with men in likeness to us, yet without sin. For he was born in Bethlehem according to flesh, as it befitted God, heavenly angels recognizing their own Lord, and praising God wrapped in swaddling clothes in a manger, and saying: Glory in the highest to God, and on earth peace to men of good will. In Nazareth he was nourished. Sitting in the midst of Teachers, he showed himself to be God, and moved admiration in them over wisdom beyond the time of age, according to body, as the Evangelical discourse narrates. He was baptized in the Jordan, not that he might assume sanctification, but that he might dispense participation in sanctification to others. In the desert he was tempted, not subjected to temptation: but he opposed our temptations to the provocation of the tempter; that he might demonstrate the tempter to be empty. On account of this he says: Be of good courage, I have overcome the world. Not opposing a divine struggle; but showing his own flesh victorious over passion, and death, and corruption: that through which flesh sin entered into the world, and through sin death reigned in all men; through the same flesh according to likeness, sin might be condemned in flesh; and the ruler of sin who tempts might be overcome; and death might be dissolved, lest it reign; and corruption might vanish in the burial of the body; and the firstfruits of resurrection might be shown, and the beginning of righteousness in the world might be exercised through faith; and the kingdom of heavens might be announced to men, and communion of God with men might be entered upon. For this grace let us glorify the Father, who gave his only-begotten Son for the life of the world: let us glorify the Holy Spirit, who works in us and vivifies us, and bestows charisms for entering upon communion with God: and lest we search out the Evangelical doctrine curiously with dry words, carrying about endless questions and battles of words; and making rough the plain and easy and right discourse concerning faith: but rather let us work the work of faith, let us love peace, let us prefer concord, let us keep unity and conjunction, let us cultivate charity, through which God is placated. Just as however it is not ours to know times or moments which the Father placed in his own power; but it is necessary to believe that there will be an end of this time, and a future manifestation of the coming age, and a revelation of judgment, and an advent of the Son of God, and a repayment of works, and a possession of the inheritance of the kingdom of heavens: so it is not ours to know how the Son of God was made man. For this mystery is great, just as it is written, Who shall narrate his generation? because his life is taken from the earth. But it is necessary to believe that the Son of God was made man according to the Scriptures; and that he was seen on earth, and conversed with men, as the Scriptures teach, in likeness to us, without sin; and that he died for us, and rose from the dead, as it is written; and that he was taken up into heavens, and sits at the right hand of the Father, whence he is about to come to judge the living and the dead, as Scripture teaches: lest perhaps while we contend with words among ourselves, some may blaspheme the doctrine of faith; and that may happen which was said: On account of you my name is always blasphemed among the nations.

pass_b_english: Let anyone who says that Christ appeared in the world only in opinion and fictitiously, and who does not confess that he came in the flesh, be anathema. How can anyone claim that Christ appeared supposedly and fictitiously to the world — Christ, I say, born in Bethlehem, brought to the circumcision of the flesh, carried by Simeon, raised by his parents up to his twelfth year, and obedient to them; baptized in the Jordan, nailed to the cross, and raised from the dead? Therefore, when it is said: He was troubled in spirit, he was saddened in soul, he was wounded in body, these are the names of the passions according to the constitution of our nature, so as to show that he was born a man in the world, and lived among men in our likeness, yet without sin. For he was born in Bethlehem according to the flesh, as was fitting for God, with the heavenly angels recognizing their Lord, and praising God wrapped in swaddling clothes in a manger, and saying: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will (Luke 2:14). He was nurtured in Nazareth. Sitting in the midst of the Teachers, he showed himself to be God, and moved them to wonder at his wisdom beyond the time of his age, according to the flesh, as the Gospel account narrates. He was baptized in the Jordan, not to receive sanctification for himself, but so that he might dispense to others a share in sanctification. He was tempted in the wilderness, yet not overcome by the temptation, but set our temptations against the tempter’s provocation, so as to show the tempter to be empty. Therefore he says: Take courage, I have conquered the world (John 16:33). He did not oppose a divine struggle, but displayed his own flesh victorious over passion, and death, and corruption: so that through the very flesh by which sin entered the world, and through sin death reigned in all people (Romans 5:12), through the same flesh according to likeness, sin might be condemned in the flesh (Romans 8:3); and the ruler of sin who tempts might be conquered; and death might be dissolved, so that it would not reign; and corruption might vanish in the burial of the body; and the firstfruits of the resurrection might be shown (1 Corinthians 15:20), and the beginning of justice in the world might be exercised through faith; and the kingdom of heaven might be announced to people, and communion of God with people might be entered. For this grace let us glorify the Father, who gave his only-begotten Son for the life of the world; let us glorify the Holy Spirit, who works in us and gives us life, and grants gifts for entering into communion with God; and let us not search out the Gospel teaching curiously with dry words, carrying around endless questions and battles of words, and making a plain and easy and right discourse about faith rough; but rather let us work the work of faith, love peace, prefer concord, keep unity and joining together, cultivate love, by which God is placated. Just as it is not ours to know the times or moments which the Father has placed in his own power (Acts 1:7); yet we must believe that there will be an end of this age, and a future manifestation of the coming age, and a revelation of judgment, and the coming of the Son of God (Acts 1:11), and the repayment of works (2 Corinthians 5:10), and the possession of the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 25:34): so it is not ours to know how the Son of God became man. For this is a great mystery, just as it is written: Who shall narrate his generation? because his life is taken from the earth (Isaiah 53:8). But we must believe that the Son of God became man according to the Scriptures; and that he was seen on earth, and lived among men, as the Scriptures teach, in our likeness, without sin; and that he died for us, and rose from the dead, as it is written; and that he was taken up into heaven, and sits at the right hand of the Father, from where he will come to judge the living and the dead, as Scripture teaches: lest perhaps while we contend with words among ourselves, some may blaspheme the doctrine of faith; and what is said may happen: Because of you my name is always blasphemed among the nations (Isaiah 52:5; Romans 2:24; Ezekiel 36:20-23).

problems.why: He was tempted but not overcome by it. English suggests he was not liable to temptation.
problems.fix: He was tempted in the wilderness, yet not overcome by the temptation, but set our temptations against the tempter’s provocation.
problems.ruling: "non subiectus tentationi" means not subjected to or overcome by temptation, in contrast with "tentatus est"; "not subject to temptation" can read as not liable to it, which misleads.

edits.old: He was tempted in the wilderness, not subject to temptation, but opposing our temptations against the tempter's provocation, so as to show the tempter to be empty.

fixed: Changed 'not subject to temptation' to 'yet not overcome by the temptation' to match 'non subiectus tentationi' (not overcome by/subdued by temptation) and the following contrast with 'obiciens' (opposing/setting against).

last_rejected.quote: He did not oppose a divine struggle
last_rejected.why: Opponens with the accusative means he did not set a divine contest against the foe, not that he refrained from resisting one.
last_rejected.fix: He did not set a divine struggle in opposition, but showed his own flesh victorious over passion, death, and corruption.
last_rejected.ruling: "Non divinam luctationem opponens; sed propriam carnem... ostendens" means he set no divine struggle against the foe but showed his flesh. English "did not oppose a divine struggle" is ambiguous, not wrong.
